strengths: The core idea of using the Gaussian splatting rendering error (computed in ResNet feature space) as a feedback signal for a gradient-free, weight-sharing recurrent update network is elegant, well-motivated by the learning-to-optimize literature, and cleanly differentiates the work from prior gradient-based refinement methods (G3R, QuickSplat) and single-step refinement (SplatFormer).

The 16x subsampled Gaussian representation with kNN + global attention for 3D context aggregation is a practical contribution in its own right, addressing the scalability limits of per-pixel feed-forward models; the compression-factor ablation (Table 4) meaningfully justifies the design choice.

Strong and comprehensive empirical evidence: three distinct evaluation protocols (8-view and 16-view DL3DV, 2-view RealEstate10K), re-training of key baselines for fairness, timing measured on the same hardware, and useful generalization analyses (cross-dataset, cross-resolution) that directly support the claim that the feedback loop improves robustness to distribution shift.

Ablations are thorough and honestly reported: e.g., the recurrent model without rendering error performs identically to initialization, cleanly isolating the contribution of the feedback signal, and kNN attention is shown to be essential for the subsampled regime.
Clear limitations section identifying kNN attention cost and saturation after three iterations; code and pre-trained models are promised for reproducibility.
weaknesses: A substantial part of the headline gains comes from the initial reconstruction model rather than the recurrent refinement: on 8-view DL3DV (Table 1), iteration 0 already reaches 26.21 PSNR vs. DepthSplat's 24.17, while recurrence adds only ~+0.6 dB at ~2x the reconstruction time (0.311s vs. 0.190s). The paper would benefit from a clearer decomposition of the gains and a comparison against a stronger single-step baseline with matched compute (e.g., more attention blocks in the initial model).

The claim that the feedback signal lets the model 'adapt to unseen data distributions at test time' is somewhat overstated: the model is frozen at test time and simply conditions on rendering error; there is no test-time adaptation or optimization in the usual sense. The improved cross-dataset/cross-resolution results are consistent with a learned iterative solver being more robust, but the framing could mislead readers.

The 'arbitrarily iterable' motivation is undercut by the empirical finding that the model saturates after 3 iterations, plausibly (as the authors admit) because the number of Gaussians is fixed. This limits the promised accuracy-speed trade-off and the test-time-compute scaling story.

The method requires ground-truth input views at test time and renders all N input views at every iteration, so the approach is tied to the sparse multi-view setup with posed cameras; dependence on camera accuracy and behavior with noisy poses is not evaluated.

The initial model is heavily built on DepthSplat (including its depth prediction backbone), and the recurrent design borrows standard components (kNN attention from Point Transformer, RAFT-style iterative updates); while the combination is novel and effective, the conceptual novelty relative to prior learning-to-optimize work is incremental.

Minor issues: several typos/grammar problems ('gradient decent', 'Be default', 'In contract'), the project page URL is blank in the abstract, and the ViT-B model (223M parameters) is much larger than the baselines it beats on efficiency metrics; parameter counts are only disclosed late in the paper.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: using the Gaussian splatting rendering error of input views as a gradient-free feedback signal to drive a weight-sharing recurrent refinement is a natural but non-obvious adaptation of the 'learning to optimize' paradigm (RAFT-style) to feed-forward Gaussian splatting, and it is well positioned against related work (G3R, SplatFormer, LIFe-GOM, QuickSplat).

The 16× subsampled 3D space with kNN + global attention context aggregation is a sensible and empirically validated design: Table 1 and Table 5(a) show it retains quality with 16× fewer Gaussians and 4× faster rendering than per-pixel baselines (MVSplat, DepthSplat), addressing a real scalability limitation of existing feed-forward models.

The experimental evidence is broad and generally convincing: three evaluation setups (8-view DL3DV at 512×960, 16-view DL3DV at 540×960 vs. Long-LRM, 2-view RealEstate10K), strong PSNR/SSIM gains (e.g., +2.6 dB over DepthSplat, outperforming Long-LRM with 4× fewer Gaussians, SOTA on RealEstate10K among feed-forward 3DGS methods), plus generalization studies (cross-dataset, cross-resolution) that directly support the test-time adaptation claim.

The ablations (compression factor, initial model, recurrent model with/without rendering error, ResNet features, attention types) substantiate the main design claims, including the indispensable role of the rendering error signal.

The paper is well written and organized; the method is described at a level of detail (architecture sizes, training schedules, losses, hyperparameters) that supports reproducibility, and code/pre-trained models are promised.
A meaningful limitations section is provided, identifying the kNN attention cost bottleneck and the saturation after three iterations.
weaknesses: The evaluation setup makes the 3DGS comparison somewhat favorable: optimization-based 3DGS with only 4K iterations and 8 views is a weak strawman for sparse-view settings, and the +3.3 dB headline claim over 3DGS should be tempered by this choice.

LPIPS results are not uniformly superior: in Table 2 (16 views), ReSplat's LPIPS (0.293–0.307) is worse than Scaffold-GS (0.250), Mip-Splatting (0.274), and even Long-LRM at iteration 0 (0.292); the 'state-of-the-art' claim in the abstract is therefore metric-dependent and should be stated more carefully.

The initial reconstruction is essentially a modified DepthSplat, and the recurrent update follows established learning-to-optimize recipes (RAFT-like recurrent field updates); the novelty is in the combination and the rendering-error feedback rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, which limits conceptual depth for a top venue.

The cross-dataset generalization claim would be stronger with a broader set of unseen datasets beyond RealEstate10K (which the authors themselves note is 'easier'), and there is no comparison against other recent feed-forward methods (e.g., NoPoSplat, FreeSplat, Flash3D) in the DL3DV setups.

The 2-view RealEstate10K setup uses a different architecture configuration (4× subsampling, 4 Gaussians per point), so the method is not a single unified model across setups; this heterogeneity is only briefly mentioned and weakens the scalability narrative.

Test-time adaptation requires rendering input views and extracting ResNet features at every iteration, which adds inference cost not fully itemized (recon. time grows from 0.31s to 0.69s over 3 iterations); a breakdown of where the recurrent gain comes from vs. simply more compute would help.
Training requires substantial resources (up to 16 GH200 GPUs with progressive multi-stage training), which, while disclosed, limits practical reproducibility for many labs.

Minor presentation issues: the project page URL in the abstract is empty; Table 5(b) reports the 'w/o render error' ablation identically to the initialization, which is expected but confusingly presented; some typos ('gradient decent', 'In contract', 'Be default').

strengths: The core idea is well motivated and original: using the Gaussian splatting rendering error (computed in feature space) as a gradient-free feedback signal to drive a weight-sharing recurrent update network is an elegant 'learning to optimize' formulation for view synthesis, and it clearly differentiates the work from G3R (explicit gradients), SplatFormer (single-step refinement), and prior recurrent methods that rely on feature correlations.

The 16× subsampled Gaussian initialization is a substantial and well-executed contribution in its own right: it reduces the number of Gaussians by 16× versus per-pixel models (MVSplat/DepthSplat) while actually improving quality, enabled by kNN + global attention for 3D context aggregation. The ablations (Table 5a) convincingly show that kNN attention is what recovers the quality lost from compression.

Comprehensive and convincing experimental evidence: three evaluation regimes (8-view and 16-view DL3DV at high resolution, and the standard 2-view RealEstate10K benchmark), consistent state-of-the-art results (e.g., +2.65 dB over re-trained DepthSplat on DL3DV, outperforming Long-LRM with 4× fewer Gaussians), plus dedicated cross-dataset and cross-resolution generalization experiments that directly support the claim that the rendering-error feedback improves robustness at test time.

Good analysis section: compression factor trade-off study (Table 4), model component ablations, timing breakdowns (recon vs. render), and a flexible accuracy/speed trade-off at inference (variable number of iterations with a single model).

The paper is clearly written, the method is well illustrated (Fig. 2), key design choices (feature-space error, error propagation via global attention, exponential loss weighting) are explained with rationale, and the authors commit to releasing code, models, and scripts, which aids reproducibility. Limitations (kNN scalability, saturation after 3 iterations, fixed Gaussian count) are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: The efficiency claims deserve more careful framing: while rendering is 4× faster than per-pixel baselines, ReSplat's total reconstruction time (0.311–0.693 s) is actually slower than MVSplat (0.129 s) and DepthSplat (0.190 s) in Table 1, largely due to kNN attention. The headline efficiency story emphasizes Gaussian count and render speed, which is fair, but the end-to-end latency trade-off (3 recurrent iterations nearly double total time) should be stated more explicitly.

The recurrent mechanism saturates after only ~3 iterations, which weakens the 'approaching the behavior of an infinitely deep network' and test-time-compute-scaling narrative. The authors' own hypothesis (fixed Gaussian count) is plausible but unverified; an experiment with adaptive or densified updates, even preliminary, would have substantiated the iterative-scaling claim.

The 'w/o render error' ablation in Table 5b yields exactly the initialization numbers (26.77/0.865/0.142). The text says no obvious improvement was observed without the rendering error, which implies the recurrent model learns essentially zero updates when the feedback signal is removed. This is an important finding (it strongly supports the paper's core thesis) but is under-analyzed; a brief explanation of why updates collapse without the error signal would strengthen the evidence for the paper's central claim.

Minor inconsistencies and gaps: the introduction states '+4.7 dB' PSNR improvement on DL3DV, which does not match any baseline pair in Table 1 (gaps are 2.65 dB over DepthSplat and ~4.3 dB over MVSplat); comparison with 3DGS is on re-optimized baselines at a hand-picked 4K-iteration budget (reasonable, but the sensitivity to this choice is not shown); and baseline results in Table 2 are borrowed from Long-LRM's paper rather than re-run.

Generalization experiments (Fig. 4) show qualitative improvements on unseen datasets/resolutions, but only PSNR curves are provided without tables including baselines under the same protocol, making it hard to quantify how much of the gain is attributable to the recurrent refinement versus the stronger initialization model.

Dependence on the DepthSplat architecture (including its depth predictor and monocular branch, 209M parameters) makes it difficult to disentangle how much of the performance comes from the recurrent design versus inheriting a stronger backbone; a more architecture-neutral recurrent study would better isolate the contribution.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and original: using the Gaussian splatting rendering error of input views as a gradient-free feedback signal to drive a weight-sharing recurrent refinement network is a clean instantiation of the 'learning to optimize' paradigm for view synthesis, and it is clearly differentiated from prior work (G3R, SplatFormer, DeepView).

The 16× subsampled Gaussian representation with kNN + global attention compensating for the reduced density is a valuable contribution in its own right, addressing the scalability limits of per-pixel feed-forward Gaussian models; the ablation (Table 6c) convincingly shows kNN attention is essential to this compression.

Experiments are extensive and well-designed: three benchmarks (DL3DV, RealEstate10K, ACID), multiple view counts and resolutions, cross-dataset/cross-view/cross-resolution generalization (Fig. 5), optimization vs. feed-forward refinement from identical initializations (Table 8), comparison with SplatFormer (Table 10), depth-regularized sparse-view 3DGS (Table 11), and recurrent vs. non-recurrent architecture ablations (Table 9).

Results are strong: state-of-the-art or near-SOTA quality with 16× fewer Gaussians and much faster reconstruction than per-scene optimization, and the model flexibly trades off accuracy and speed via the number of iterations with a single set of weights.

The paper is clearly written, the method is described in enough detail to reproduce (including losses, training schedule, coordinate-system analysis), and the authors commit to releasing code, models, and scripts. Limitations (kNN scaling, saturation after 4 iterations) are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: The method requires ground-truth input views and COLMAP poses at both training and test time; the feedback loop is fundamentally limited by assuming accurate poses and available reference imagery, and the paper does not discuss sensitivity to pose noise or potential in-the-wild applicability.

Scalability concerns remain: the kNN attention makes the recurrent step expensive as the point count grows (already slower than Long-LRM in the 16-view setup), so the claimed efficiency advantage does not uniformly hold across regimes.

A single model cannot yet serve all settings: compression factor (16× vs. 4×) is chosen per setup, and training uses progressive multi-stage fine-tuning per dataset/resolution, which complicates the generality narrative; the 2-view RealEstate10K variant decodes 4 Gaussians per point, diverging from the '16× fewer Gaussians' headline claim.

Several presentation issues reduce confidence: Table 8 contains an obvious typo (SSIM 0.960 for 20 iterations), the project-page URL is empty, and in Table 7 the test views differ across view-count configurations, making the 8/16/32-view comparison with 3DGS not strictly on equal footing.

The SplatFormer comparison required substantial adaptation (grid search over serialization grids) by the authors, so the reported 2dB gap may understate SplatFormer's potential; a stronger independent baseline would be reassuring. Similarly, comparisons to 3DGS at 32 views show the gap narrowing as inputs increase (Table 7).
No user study or perceptual quality assessment beyond PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS; given the paper's claims of visually sharper results, this is a minor omission but would strengthen the evidence.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: using the Gaussian splatting rendering error of the input views as a gradient-free feedback signal for a weight-sharing recurrent refinement network. This is a sensible adaptation of the 'learning to optimize' paradigm (RAFT-style recurrency) to feed-forward 3D Gaussian prediction, and it is cleanly distinguished from related work (G3R, SplatFormer, LIFe-GOM, QuickSplat).

The compact 16x-subsampled Gaussian representation is a practical contribution in its own right, addressing a real scalability problem of per-pixel feed-forward models (millions of Gaussians), and the kNN + global attention design for compensating the information loss is validated by ablation (Table 6c).

Experiments are extensive and well-organized: three evaluation setups (8-view 512x960 DL3DV, 16-view 540x960 DL3DV following Long-LRM, 2-view RealEstate10K/ACID), multiple baselines re-trained or compared under consistent protocols, and generalization tests across unseen datasets, view counts, and resolutions (Fig. 5).

The ablation study is thorough and supports the design choices: rendering error ablation (Table 6a), coordinate system choice, compression factor trade-off (Table 5), recurrent vs. non-recurrent weight-sharing architectures (Table 9), comparison with SplatFormer (Table 10), depth-regularized 3DGS optimization (Table 11), feature extractor choice (Table 12), and runtime profiling (Table 13).

The paper is honest about limitations (kNN attention cost at >500K Gaussians, saturation after 4 iterations), promises code/model release, and includes an LLM usage statement. The optimization-based vs. feed-forward refinement comparison (Fig. 4, Table 8) from a shared initialization is a particularly fair and informative experiment.
weaknesses: Attribution of gains between the two contributions is somewhat confounded. At iteration 0 the initial model already improves substantially over DepthSplat (26.21 vs 24.17 in Table 1) due to architectural/training changes beyond mere compression; the recurrent module adds a further ~1.5dB. A more careful decomposition (e.g., initialization retrained at full per-pixel resolution) would strengthen the claim that both components are necessary.

The 'adaptation to unseen test distributions' narrative should be interpreted with care: the feedback loop requires ground-truth input views, which are available for reconstruction but the method does not perform true test-time optimization; the generalization gains, while demonstrated, are bounded and the model still saturates after only 4 iterations.

The method is architecture-dependent on DepthSplat (backbone, depth predictor) and the recurrent module is built from established components (kNN attention, global attention, pixel shuffle/unshuffle); the novelty is primarily in the recurrent formulation and the rendering-error feedback rather than new building blocks.

Some practical caveats: reconstruction time is slower than Long-LRM due to the kNN operation (acknowledged), evaluation is confined to forward-facing/video-derived scene datasets (DL3DV, RealEstate10K, ACID), and Table 8 contains an apparent typo (SSIM 0.960 for 'ReSplat(init)+3DGS, 20 iter', inconsistent with surrounding values) that should be corrected.

The claim of SOTA is solid but margins on some benchmarks (e.g., vs. LVSM dec-only on RealEstate10K, where LVSM has no explicit 3D representation) are modest, and the speed comparison there depends on rendering-time arguments rather than reconstruction quality alone.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: using the Gaussian splatting rendering error of input views as a gradient-free feedback signal for a weight-sharing recurrent update network is an elegant application of 'learning to optimize' to feed-forward view synthesis, and is convincingly differentiated from prior work (SplatFormer, G3R, QuickSplat, LIFe-GOM) in both the related work section and dedicated appendix comparisons (Table 10).

The 16x-subsampled Gaussian representation addresses a genuine scalability problem of per-pixel feed-forward models; the ablations (Table 6c, Table 5) show the design is not trivial and that kNN + global attention is needed to compensate for the reduced capacity.

Comprehensive and largely convincing empirical evidence: three evaluation setups (8-view and 16-view DL3DV at high resolution, 2-view RealEstate10K/ACID), direct comparisons against re-trained baselines (3DGS, MVSplat, DepthSplat), comparisons with Long-LRM and GS-LRM/LVSM, plus an explicit optimization-based vs. feed-forward refinement comparison starting from the same initialization (Fig. 4, Table 8) that cleanly isolates the benefit of the learned recurrent update.

Strong generalization analysis (cross-dataset, cross-view-count, cross-resolution, Fig. 5) that supports the central claim that the rendering-error feedback improves robustness to distribution shift, and thorough ablations covering the error representation, coordinate system, compression factor, and recurrent architecture (including weight-sharing vs. stacked/deeper non-recurrent variants, Table 9).

Good transparency and reproducibility posture: model profiling (Table 13), training details, a limitations paragraph (kNN attention cost, saturation after 4 iterations), an LLM usage statement, and a commitment to release code, models, and scripts.
weaknesses: The claim that the feedback signal 'naturally adapts to unseen data distributions at test time' is somewhat overstated: the rendering error is computed only on the input views, which the model already fits well, so the adaptation is indirect (via improved geometry/consistency) rather than true test-time optimization on target views. The generalization gains are real, but the mechanism explanation could be more precise.

Some fairness caveats in the headline comparisons: the DL3DV model is progressively fine-tuned with 16 views at 512x960, and 3DGS baselines are capped at 4K iterations (justified by overfitting, but sensitivity to this choice is not shown); on 16-view DL3DV, ReSplat's reconstruction time is slower than Long-LRM's, and the results at iteration 0 in Table 2 are essentially on par with Long-LRM, meaning most of the gain comes from the recurrent steps — the setup descriptions could be more explicit.

Minor internal inconsistencies and presentation issues that should be fixed: Table 8 reports SSIM 0.960 for ReSplat(init)+3DGS at 20 iterations, which is almost certainly a typo (all neighboring values are ~0.85); the project page URL is empty; Table 6c shows the compressed initial model has better PSNR but worse LPIPS than DepthSplat, which is not discussed.

Several key design choices are empirical rather than analyzed: why the middle view coordinate frame helps (+0.9dB) is only hypothesized, the saturation after 4 iterations is not explained, and the two-view RealEstate10K setup switches to a different scheme (4x subsampling with 4 Gaussians per point), so the 2-view results do not directly test the 16x-compression idea that is central to the paper.

The initial reconstruction model is essentially DepthSplat with subsampling plus point-cloud attention layers; the architectural novelty is modest and the paper's contribution rests mainly on the recurrent refinement framework — this is acceptable, but the writing occasionally frames well-established components (ResNet features, kNN attention, pixel unshuffle tricks) as if they were novel.
